subject: bauhausBird
pitch:
Category: Animal.
Subject: songbird on a branch.
Style: Bauhaus primary-colour geometry.

spec.name: Bauhaus Songbird
spec.description: A small songbird perched on a short branch, built from circles, triangles and rectangles in red, yellow, blue, black and white, in the style of a Bauhaus poster.
spec.layout: Real songbird scale (about 12 cm of bird on a 44 cm branch). The branch lies along X, resting on the floor with its top at y=0.036. The bird perches on it centred at x=0 and faces +Z. Body axis is tilted about 30° (breast up and forward, rump low), with the tail trailing back and slightly down. The head is a big round yellow ball sitting almost neckless on the top-front of the body. The beak is short and conical, red, split into separate upper and lower jaws. From front to back: beak tip at z≈0.125, then the head, then the red chest disc, the blue back and white belly, the folded wings, and the black/blue/yellow barred tail ending at z≈-0.145. Short black legs with 3 forward toes and 1 hind toe grip the branch top. The only forms are discs, spheres, cones, flat triangles and rectangles. Every colour block has a hard edge, and no part is covered in decoration. Colour roles: yellow head, blue back, red chest disc and wings, white belly, black ink for outlines, bars, legs and tail. Each coloured disc or emblem sits on a slightly larger black disc, 1.5 mm proud of the surface, as a poster-style outline. All colours are flat, with no gradients and no paint. Left is +X, and L joints and parts are at +X. Mirror every paired part for R at -X. Rest pose: wings folded but slightly separated from the body, beak closed, legs apart, toes spread.

parts.builds: The body and its colour blocking. The body is a low-poly ellipsoid about 0.16 long along the body bone and 0.05 radius, a swept or lofted egg shape riding the body and neck joints. The back and top are blue (sectors or a separate cap). The lower half is a white belly with a hard horizontal edge, kept as a separate shape. A big red disc (radius about 0.028) with a black outline disc behind it sits on the breast at chestFront, facing forward and slightly up. A yellow triangle sits on the rump, a black collar ring or band marks where the neck meets the body, and a thin blueDeep saddle stripe runs across the shoulders. Small geometric accents repeat the motif: a yellowDeep square at each flank and 2 or 3 small white or black discs along the belly edge. The body carries the neck joint, and the neck can be a short blue cylinder or sweep that hides the join with the head. It does NOT build wings, legs, tail or head.
parts.attaches: Head sits on top of the front at neckBase and headCentre. Wings meet at shoulderL and shoulderR on the flanks. Tail starts at tailRoot on the rump. Legs emerge from the belly at hipL and hipR.

parts.builds: A round yellow head (low-poly sphere, radius about 0.032, centred at headCentre) with a yellowDeep cap disc or crown ring. The beak is a separate upper jaw (red cone or wedge, about 0.03 long) and a lower jaw (a smaller redDeep cone). It is built at beakBase, hinged at jawHinge, with the jaw riding the jaw joint and the upper beak riding head. A black line marks the mouth. Two big eyes sit on the sides and show from the front: a black outline disc, then a white disc, a blue iris disc and a black pupil, each layered 1 mm apart, and a tiny white highlight. A black brow bar over each eye. A blue circle cheek patch behind each eye, and a crest of three flat triangular blades on the crown (red, blue and black, tallest in the middle, fanned fore-to-aft). A small black dot nostril on each side of the upper beak. Nothing blocks the eyes or beak from the front.
parts.attaches: Sits on the body top-front at headCentre and neckBase. The beak tip is the foremost point of the model at z≈0.125.

parts.builds: Both folded wings, mirrored, and the tail. Each wing is a red rounded-triangle or quarter-disc covert slab on the flank (extrude, riding wingL1/wingR1 and wingL2/wingR2), with a black outline slab behind it. Below it are 4 long flight-feather blades in a stepped fan (blue, yellow, blue, black, each a thin extruded elongated rectangle or triangle with a pointed tip). A yellow disc and a white bar sit on the covert, and the tips end in alternating black and white squares. The wings lie slightly apart from the body, tips near [±0.095, 0.085, -0.115]. The tail has 5 flat feather blades (extruded long rectangles with a notched or pointed tip) fanned slightly, colours black, blue, black, blue, black, with a yellow band stripe and a red tip triangle on the middle feather, and a white bar across all feathers. It sweeps back and slightly down from tailRoot to a tip at about [0, 0.058, -0.145], riding tail1 and tail2.
parts.attaches: Wings attach at shoulderL and shoulderR on the body flanks. The tail starts at tailRoot under the rump triangle.

parts.builds: Both legs, mirrored. Each has a rounded thigh puff (a small sphere at hip, white on the inner side and yellowDeep on the outside), a thin black tarsus rod from hip to ankle, a red ring band at the ankle (a small cylinder), and a foot with 3 forward toes and 1 hind toe. Each toe is a thin black rod or capsule of 3-4 mm radius, about 0.02 long, spread and gripping across the top of the branch (toes lie at y≈0.040 and curve slightly down at the tips). Each toe ends in a small red cone claw, and each knuckle has a tiny yellow disc. The legs are about 4 cm apart. Everything rides the matching leg and toe joints.
parts.attaches: Hips attach at hipL and hipR on the belly. Feet rest on the branch top at perchTop (y=0.036), toes touching it.

parts.builds: The perch. A straight, slightly tapered rod along X from x=-0.22 to x=0.22 (radius about 0.016, axis at y=0.02, bottom touching the floor, top at 0.036) in branchDark. Colour bands, as short slightly larger cylinder rings, repeat red, yellow, blue and white at set spacing, with the middle 0.07 left plain under the bird's feet. The ends are flat black cut discs with a white inner ring. A short forked twig rises from the left end region (+X, around x=0.15) at about 50°, with a smaller twig branching from it, made of black rods with colour-ring bands. The twigs carry geometric leaves: a red disc, a yellow triangle, a blue half-disc and a white square, each on its own black outline shape. A small knot disc and 2 stub nubs sit along the main branch. A second short stub rises on the right end (-X) with a blue disc leaf. Twigs stay below y=0.16 and clear of the bird. Everything rides the perch joint.
parts.attaches: The branch top at perchTop (y=0.036, x=0) is where the toes land. It is the lowest part of the model and rests on the floor.

calls.reasoning:
I'm sketching out the concrete proportions for a songbird perched on a branch, using Bauhaus-style primary color geometry — figuring real-world scale (bird ~14cm, branch ~35cm) and deciding orientation, with the branch running along X and the bird facing +Z.

For materials, I'm assigning Bauhaus primaries: a blue body, yellow head, red wing and beak accents, black tail bars, and white/cream for belly and eye details, with the branch rendered as a black rod with colored bands. Now I'm starting to break the creature down into skeletal parts, beginning with the torso.

I'm splitting the model into five parts — body, head, wings/tail, legs/feet, and branch — budgeting roughly 140 units each within a ~700 total. I'm working out the perched posture, tilting the body axis forward with the head raised and tail dipped behind, placing joints at the hips, branch-top contact, and head/body centers accordingly.

The overall bounding box comes out to roughly 0.44 wide, 0.22 tall, 0.27 deep, keeping the beak, tail tip, and head top within those limits while centering the branch and body along the z-axis. I'm setting the root joint for the body at its center point to anchor the rest of the skeleton.

Now I'm building the joint chain: root body, then neck parented to it with a forward-upward direction, then head parented to neck, then a jaw hinge parented to head positioned at the base of the beak where the lower mandible would pivot.

Then I'm adding the tail as two segments trailing backward-downward from the body, and the wings as shoulder-to-tip chains parented at the body, held folded but angled slightly outward (~25°) from the body in rest pose to keep the limbs visually separated.

For the legs, I'm laying out hip, ankle, and foot joints running down from the body, with the foot splitting into forward-facing digits plus a rear hallux toe, keeping the bird anatomy believable with hidden thigh and visible tarsus.

For the feet, I'm having the toes curve downward on either side of a branch to simulate gripping — joints parented to the foot bone, with the branch itself kept as a static, separate prop that doesn't follow the bird's rig.

Now I need to figure out the root joint issue: since a rigged model requires exactly one root, I'm debating whether the branch should ride that root or stay fully external. I'm leaning toward naming the root joint something like "perch" positioned near the feet, though I'm unsure whether to assign it a role from the allowed list or leave it unset, since misassigning a role could confuse the rig hierarchy.

Now I'm settling on a Bauhaus-inspired palette: primary red, yellow, and blue, paired with black, white, and cream neutrals, plus deeper shade variants for contrast, and I'm considering a warm grey or muted wood tone for the branch and legs to keep the geometric color-blocking feel consistent.

I'm mapping color blocks onto the bird's anatomy: a blue back, white belly, red semicircle chest patch, yellow sphere head with a black eye ring, a red wing slab with blue and yellow geometric accents, black tail rectangles with blue/yellow tip stripes, black legs with red claws, and a two-tone beak split between black and red.

Now I'm breaking the build into parts: starting with the torso as a loft/ellipsoid shape with blue back, white belly, red chest disc, yellow rump triangle, black collar band, and shoulder accents, bounded within a defined joint box and poly budget, then moving to the head as a sphere/cube hybrid with beak jaws and layered eye discs.

For wings and tail, I'm planning red covert quarter-discs plus stacked flight feather blades in blue/yellow/black with banding, and a five-blade tail alternating colors, all within a joint box covering both wings and tail with their own poly budget. Next I'm sketching legs and feet, including tarsi and thigh feather trousers.

For the branch, I'm designing a dark main rod with colored bands, forked twigs, geometric leaf discs and triangles, a cut-end disc, knots, and a rising twig with foliage near one end, keeping it grounded as the base while the bird perches above. Totaling the poly budget across all parts, it comes to 750, which works, so now I'm setting up the mount points starting with the top of the perch.

Now I'm working through the skeletal mount positions for hips, feet, neck, head, beak, shoulders, tail, and chest, then defining the body as an ellipsoid tilted to follow the spine's angle.

Checking that the head overlaps the body front-top smoothly, giving a neckless songbird look. Now I'm positioning the legs: hips near the belly, short feathered thighs, tarsus dropping down to toes resting just above the branch surface, with hip, ankle, and foot joints placed to keep the pose compact and grounded.

Now I'm laying out the toe joints per foot, planning single-joint digits (three forward, one hind) mirrored across left and right sides to keep the skeleton economical while still covering the full joint list: perch, body, neck, head, jaw, tail segments, and wings.

Writing JSON joints...

I'll confirm left is +X in model-space, then lay out the description using the shared motifs of circles, triangles, and squares/bars—rendering everything as discs, cones, and boxes with flat colors and thin black ink outlines (black disc behind each colored one). I'll write it concisely but with full color names and detail before finalizing the output.

I'm working out how to build the leg and foot geometry using the existing joints, planning the hip, ankle, and foot positions and how to connect them with rods or capsules.

Now I'm figuring out the toe directions and lengths for each foot—three forward toes and one hind toe per side, mirrored for left and right—and checking that the toe tips sit properly against the branch surface so they look like they're gripping it, accounting for the branch's curved radius versus the toes' forward reach.

Adding toe joint details...

Now working out the thigh structure: a rod bone from hip to ankle, and a puffy hip sphere split into two colored hemispheres (white inner, deep yellow outer) using partial sphere geometries.

Working out the rotations so each hemisphere faces outward correctly — rotating by +90°/-90° around Y to orient the yellow and white halves for left and right eyes, with the seam between them left unaddressed since the closed sphere hides it. Now I'm moving on to the ankle ring, a small red cylinder.

I'm adding thin black outline rings above and below the ankle marker for contrast, then extending the leg structure down to the foot with a short capsule joint and a small black sphere as the foot pad.

Now I'm placing a hip puff sphere and working out the toe geometry — computing normalized spread directions for four toes radiating from the foot point, with staggered lengths and downward claw tips for the hind toe.

I'm adding yellow knuckle discs atop each toe base and black outline discs beneath them for contrast, then tallying parts: roughly 21 pieces per side (puff, rods, rings, pad, toes with claws and discs) doubled for both sides, landing around 58 total components.

I'm sketching the buildHead function using the provided Ctx type, planning the head's center position and radius along with the box dimensions for the geometry.

Now I'm designing the component pieces: a yellow sphere for the head, a darker yellow spherical cap for the crown, and fanned crest blades extruded along the z-axis to sit on top, working out their exact dimensions and placement relative to the head joint.

Now I'm positioning the three blades front-to-back along z with tilt angles (+25°, 0°, -25°), seating each on the crown sphere surface and checking that the tallest middle blade's height stays within the max allowed limit.

For the upper beak, I'm working out the cone dimensions so the tip lands at z≈0.125 with the base buried in the head surface, using a spike helper that takes base/tip points and a radius with a hexagonal cross-section for a slight angular beak look.

Still working through beak geometry...

Still working out the mouth line placement...

Thinking about adding nostril dots on the upper beak sides, positioning them symmetrically near z≈0.092 based on the beak's taper profile at that point.

For the eyes, I'm calculating the direction vector from the head sphere's center using azimuth and elevation angles so each eye sits realistically on the curved surface, then layering black outline discs slightly proud of the sphere.

I'm adjusting the azimuth closer to 55° so both eyes read as visible from the front, then checking that the layered disc radii for outline, white, iris, pupil, and highlight stay within bounds on the sphere's curvature without excessive edge sag.

For the cheek patch, I'm computing a similar sag correction for its outline radius and setting proud offsets so the black border and blue fill sit correctly above the surface.

I'm checking the angular spread of the cheek and eye features to confirm they don't overlap, and verifying the cheek's z-position falls behind the sphere's front center—everything checks out fine.

Now I'm positioning the brow bar above each eye, calculating its elevation offset and sizing the box dimensions.

I'll keep the brow flat rather than angled, checking that its sag and positioning line up with the eyes below and don't overlap the cap geometry above—since the cap covers elevations above 50° and the brow sits around 34°, it should clear it fine.

Now I'm settling on using the named mount points from the spec—headCentre, beakBase, jawHinge—as [x,y,z] arrays, and starting to write a helper function to work with them.

Writing disc helper function...

For the eyes, I'm planning blue iris, black pupil, and a tiny white highlight disc offset slightly toward one side, computed by perturbing the azimuth/elevation of the eye center position.

Still positioning the crown ring...

Adjusting the lower jaw disc sizing and position, then moving on to writing the spike function calls for the beak with color and sides options for a scalene beak shape.

Thinking through the helper for extruding blade shapes like crests, defining their triangular outline with a forward-offset tip, and considering whether a black outline layer behind the crest would conflict with the main shape's thickness.

Layering colored and outline blades with slightly different sizes so the outline peeks out as a thin rim around the colored face, skipping the outline for the black blade since it's already black.

Now I'm computing crest blade positions along the curved crown using a sphere equation, placing three blades (fore, mid, aft) with different heights and tilt angles, with the fore blade tilted forward and aft tilted backward, and setting up the extrusion axes so thickness runs correctly relative to each blade's tilt.

I'm planning the buildBranch function using the Ctx type provided by the module, designing a main rod along the X axis with a tapering radius profile centered near the origin.

Adding bands and twigs...

Adjusting rod and disc end dimensions...

Now working out the twig geometry: it branches off the main branch at x=0.15, rising at roughly 50° elevation heading outward in +X with a slight Z offset to keep it clear of the bird's wingspan, with a length around 0.085 giving its tip position.

A smaller secondary twig should fork off the main one partway along at a steeper, near-80° angle for a forked look, with the main twig itself tapering from a thicker to thinner radius for a spiky rod appearance. Leaves attached at the tip need to stay under the height ceiling, which works out fine given their size, and each leaf will be built from a black-outlined shape using an extrude helper function.

Planning leaf orientation facing the viewer with thickness along the z-axis, a slightly larger black outline layer behind the colored front layer, and a thin black petiole rod connecting each leaf to the twig. For the disc and triangle shapes, using cylinder geometry oriented along the z-axis and extruded outlines respectively, keeping segment counts modest for performance.

Writing shape-scaling helper...

Adding slight rotation to the leaf outlines so they sit at an angle, then placing each leaf: a red disc at the main twig tip, a yellow triangle at the small twig tip, and a blue half-disc on a short stem branching off the main twig, all computed in model space relative to the perch bone.

Still working out exact leaf placements...

Checking the blue half-disc separation from the triangle tip, then positioning it off a twig stem so it stays within bounds and doesn't collide with other leaves on the z-axis.

Now I'm placing a second square stub off the forked twig, verifying its distance from the yellow triangle, and adding small colored ring bands along the twigs to mark growth segments using thin cylinders aligned to each twig's direction.

I'm spacing out the ring bands down the left side and adding a knot disc on the branch's front face, layering black outline, cream, and dark concentric circles, then adjusting its position to avoid overlapping a band.

Now I'm placing small stub nubs protruding from the main branch as short rods angled slightly downward and outward.

I'm considering adding thin black outline rings behind each colored band for a Bauhaus poster-style effect, bringing the part count to 26. I'm also working out a slight radius taper along the axis so the rod's lowest point just touches the floor, adjusting the axis height accordingly.

I'll try a linear taper from radius 0.0135 at the -X end to 0.0185 at +X, giving a subtle "slightly tapered" look while keeping the top near the perch at 0.036. The exact floor contact isn't critical since the bird's toes extend lower anyway, so I'll settle on this taper and move on.

I'm trying slightly flared end caps with radius a touch larger than the rod so the bottom edge grazes the floor without an obvious gap, settling on roughly 0.0195 radius caps against a 0.02 axis height to keep the sink minimal.

Then I decide to taper the rod itself linearly from 0.0155 at one end to 0.0165 at the other, defining it as a cylinder swept along the X axis with 12-16 sides and flat ends rather than rounded caps, building it as a standard part attached to the perch bone. I also plan tip "stems" as thin rods for leaf attachments.

For twigs I'll switch to a capsule helper for cleaner rounded ends, still bound to the perch joint. For extruded shapes I set up a helper taking an outline plus local x/y axes, with thickness extending along the cross product giving the z-depth, making sure outline points stay non-self-intersecting and applying rotation before extrusion -- and I start sketching half-disc point arrangements for one of these outlines.

Still writing helper functions...

Defining twig geometry and rings...

Finishing the nub geometry details...

I'm planning the wing and tail joint positions and orientations, then setting up extruded outlines to build those shapes with proper alignment.

With red proud by 1.5mm settled, I'm now working out the wing's tilt direction—since the tips lean outward and back from the shoulder, I'm computing a normalized direction vector for the wing axis and figuring out the perpendicular "up" direction needed to define the panel's orientation for extrusion.

For the right side the cross product gives the same +X direction, but outward should be -X there, so I need to flip the thickness sign for that side rather than mirroring the whole basis—just negate the offset direction when applying layers on the right.

I realize the outline shape itself is identical for both wings since it's drawn in local (u,v) coordinates, and the mirrored placement of the basis vectors automatically produces the mirror image in world space, so I don't need separate geometry for left and right wings. Now I'm thinking about bone assignments—wingL1 for coverts and main flight feathers, wingL2 for the outer feather layer.

I'm laying out the wing geometry with the shoulder as the local origin, u running along the wing axis toward the tip (around 0.13 length), and v for height perpendicular to it, starting with the covert shape as a rounded triangle near the root.

I need to make sure the shoulder point sits just outside the body ellipsoid's surface so the wing doesn't clip into the torso -- placing it slightly beyond x=0.05 and checking that the plane tilts outward correctly as it extends toward the tail without intersecting the narrowing rear of the body.

Writing covert outline coordinates...

For the black outline I'll offset each point outward from the centroid by a small fixed distance to create an even border, then move to the flight feathers—four long stepped pointed-rectangle blades fanning out below and behind the covert.

Working out the layering...

I'm adding small alternating black-and-white square tips near the ends of each feather, placed before the taper so they sit proudly on the surface, plus a yellow disc accent on the covert.

Now I'm figuring out the disc geometry with a black outline ring behind it, using a short cylinder positioned along the wing's thickness axis, then working out where to place a white bar rectangle across the covert feather so it stays within the covert's outline bounds.

Working through bone assignment: the covert spans closer to the shoulder while feathers and tip squares extend further out, so I'm assigning feathers and tip squares to wing2 and the covert/disc/bar details to wing1, since that matches their relative distances along the wing.

Now I'm calculating feather vertical placement, with centers spaced downward and angled progressively steeper for the lower feathers so the fan shape matches the tip positions near the described coordinates.

The covert sits at top, with feathers at c=-0.036 extending below it, starting from u0=0.03. I'm checking the wing's overall droop is small enough to look natural, and the rotation math for the outline points around the local origin works out. Keeping feather widths and triangle counts modest, I'm tallying parts per wing — outline, covert, disc, bar, feathers, squares — to stay within a reasonable budget.

Now I'm moving to the tail, planning 5 feathers with yellow bands, a red tip triangle on the middle one, and a white bar crossing all of them. I'm working out the tail's axis direction from root to tip and setting up the local coordinate system (tail axis, lateral, thickness) needed to extrude the tail outline correctly.

Now I'm planning the tail as a fan of five feathers at slight angles, with the center feather longest and outer ones shorter, rooted near the rump and oriented using the computed up vector for layering.

Defining feather layering and offsets...

Checking the feather taper profile confirms the triangle fits within bounds, and I verify the tail tip position lands correctly by solving for root plus offset times the direction vector.

Now I'm figuring out tail bone placement with two segments, deciding whether feathers should attach rigidly to tail1 versus tail2 so the fan doesn't break across the joint, leaning toward putting the feather geometry on tail1 and reserving tail2 for simpler banding details.

Defining feather polygon geometry...

All feathers share the same base point with slight overlap for layering, and I'm stacking layer offsets so the middle feather sits above its neighbors, with decorations positioned just above each feather's top face using small thickness increments.

I'm checking whether near the base, where feather width is 0.022 but angular spacing only yields about 0.0052 between centers, the feathers overlap substantially—essentially creating a shingled fan effect rather than clean separation.

I'm adjusting the fan geometry, trying wider angles and narrower feather widths to get a stripier, more visually distinct layered look without excessive overlap at the tips.

The overlap there looks minor and acceptable, so I'll keep layer steps simple at 0.0005. I'm considering adding a thin black outline behind the red triangle for contrast, similar to the existing black outline under the yellow wing disc, since it's cheap to add. Now I'm moving on to writing the wings and tail builder function.

Writing helper functions...

Still computing wing geometry basis vectors...

I'm working out a growth function that expands outline points outward from their centroid by a fixed amount, then thinking through the exact layer offsets and thicknesses for covert outline versus covert red fill along the normal axis so the feather layers stack correctly without z-fighting.

Now I'm working out the disc's layering—red base, black ring, yellow top—each stepped up about 1.5mm proud, then placing a white bar rectangle above those, positioning it along the u-axis so it clears the disc's radius.

Next I'm plotting the covert (wing feather) outline as a set of rounded corner points, then checking whether that shape's top edge sits outside the body's circular cross-section at the shoulder, since the covert needs to attach smoothly where the wing meets the body curve.

Still adjusting coordinates...

Working out feather lengths with each one slightly shorter and rotated at increasing downward angles so the tips sweep down, then placing small alternating black-and-white tip squares near each feather's point to match the blue/yellow/blue/black color sequence.

Setting the tip squares' thickness and vertical offset so they sit proud of the feather surface without overlapping into the covert layer, and binding feathers to a secondary bone while the covert stays on the primary one.

I'm considering adding a thin black outline slab behind each feather for a poster-style edge effect, positioning it slightly below and offset so it peeks out only around the feather's border without z-fighting, checking that neighboring feather layers still properly occlude each other's outlines.

I'll settle on a grow value of 0.0016 for the outlines, adding four parts per wing, and plan to apply the same outline technique to the tail feathers using a similar piece-building function that returns the outline polygons.

Still defining tip geometry and outline offsets...

Now I'm setting up a rotation helper to position each feather around the origin, and working out the layering order so outlines sit slightly behind each feather where they overlap near the base of the fan.

I'm checking whether the outline thickness and vertical offsets actually keep each feather's outline peeking out past the feather layered below it — right now the math shows the outline getting fully hidden by the next feather up, so I need to widen the layer step size so the outline stays visible along the edge as intended.

I notice the outer decor top is actually coplanar with the next feather's top, risking z-fighting given the overlap at that spacing — so I bump decor thickness to 0.0012 centered at l+0.0014, pushing its top to l+0.002 to clear it. Now I'm checking the wing feathers for similar step adjustments.

I'm adjusting the black outline to touch the feather top by shifting its center to 0.0040, then positioning the red layer so it sits proud by 0.0015mm over the black. From there I'm stacking the disc components—black cylinder then yellow disc—each built on top of the previous layer's top surface.

I'm tweaking the yellow cylinder's height and center so its top surface ends up proud by exactly 1.5mm, then doing the same positioning check for the white bar. These are all sub-millimeter adjustments on a wing that's only 0.13 units wide, but they're visible at this viewing scale, so I'm now moving on to size the tip squares for the wing feathers relative to their upper neighbors.

Checking whether adjacent feather squares overlap given their spacing versus width — the math shows a 4mm overlap zone in the feather geometry but the squares themselves stay within bounds, so no actual collision. I'm also sorting out which bones control the covert versus the feathers, then tallying up the total part count per wing: covert outline, covert, two discs, bar, four feathers with outlines and squares comes to 17 parts per side, doubled for both wings, and I'm starting the same count for the tail feathers.

I'm tallying the remaining tail decoration pieces — yellow band with outline, red triangle with outline, five white bars — bringing the total part count to roughly 63 against a budget of 190, leaving room to add more detail like rachis lines while still keeping the restrained Bauhaus aesthetic; I decide small extras like blue covert bases or extra wing bars aren't necessary. Now I'm working out the tail's coordinate geometry, defining the root origin, direction vectors, and an "up" vector computed from a cross product to extrude each tail layer correctly.

I'm mapping feather points using local coordinates along the tail direction and the perpendicular axis, with rotation angle determining left-right placement, then assigning tail feathers to bone joints — base pieces to the first tail joint, tips and decoration to the second — and confirming that joint exists. For color, I'm setting up an alternating black-blue-black-blue-black pattern across five feathers indexed by angle, with the center feather getting the yellow band, while double-checking how the palette's color constants are named.

For the small red triangle tip on the center feather, I'm sizing it tiny (about 0.026 long, 0.009 wide) and widening that middle feather's half-width slightly to accommodate it, deciding to skip an outline since it sits on a black feather and would be invisible anyway.

Setting tail lengths now, with the middle feather longest and shorter lengths stepping down for adjacent ones, plus mixing pointed and notched tip shapes across the fan. Still writing feather geometry...

I'll keep imports minimal, just THREE, and define a point type that supports sharp corners for the outline. I'm writing a rotation helper that transforms point arrays around an origin, preserving the sharp-corner marker, then starting a helper to scale/grow shapes.

Thinking through the growth logic more carefully though — using centroid-direction scaling would distort an elongated feather shape, since points along the sides would mostly shift lengthwise instead of sideways. So instead I'll define explicit parametric outlines for wing feathers with the growth amount baked directly into the point coordinates.

Setting up the wing/tail builder function with helper utilities for vectors and point types...

Defining the wing disc using a cylinder geometry oriented along the normal direction, with smoothing applied to covert feathers and a slight centroid growth factor for roundness, plus feather overlap tuning.

Settling on blue/yellow/black for wing feather colors, checking that the joint pieces at the covert and feather bones are rigid, and noting the unused tail frame import before finalizing the write-out.

I need to figure out how to type the Ctx parameter for buildTorso without importing it directly, since it's presumably provided globally by the module.

For the body geometry, I'm calculating the torso bone's axis direction (tilted upward and forward) and sizing an ellipsoid-like shape along that axis, making sure it stays within reasonable bounding dimensions for the ribcage/chest area.

For color blocking, I need a hard horizontal edge between the blue top and white belly even though the body is tilted — so I'm considering building a custom ellipsoid geometry by transforming sphere vertices into model space and splitting them by a world-horizontal cutoff rather than relying on a simple phi/theta sphere cut.

Belly is the local -Z side, so cutting along that axis gives an edge that runs parallel to the body's tilt, which reads naturally. I'm rotating a sphere geometry so its pole aligns with local Z instead of Y, then using the lower cap angles to carve the belly shape after working out the rotated coordinate mapping.

Using matching segment counts keeps the flat shading facets aligned between pieces.
